title: Hadza Grandmothers
text:
Humans are unusual among primates: women often live for decades after they stop being able to have children. The anthropologist Kristen Hawkes and her colleagues wondered why evolution would favor such long lives, and found a clue among the Hadza, hunter-gatherers living near Lake Eyasi in northern Tanzania.

Observing and measuring how Hadza women spent their days, the team noticed that older women were among the hardest workers in camp. They spent long hours gathering food, especially digging up deep tubers, a task too difficult for young children. Much of what they gathered went to their grandchildren and other young relatives.

The effect showed up in the children. When a mother had a new baby and could forage less, her weaned children's growth depended on how much time their grandmother spent gathering for them. A hardworking grandmother helped keep them well fed.

In a 1998 paper, Hawkes, James O'Connell, Nicholas Blurton Jones, Helen Alvarez and Eric Charnov proposed the grandmother hypothesis. In ancestral humans, they argued, older women who helped feed their grandchildren allowed their daughters to have babies more often, and their descendants thrived. Over many generations, this could have favored longer lifespans, and with them other features of human life, such as long childhoods.
lesson: Grandparents are not a footnote in family life; they may be part of why our species thrives. Draw them in and honor what they give.
people: Kristen Hawkes, James O'Connell, Nicholas Blurton Jones, Helen Alvarez, Eric Charnov
location: Hadza territory near Lake Eyasi, Tanzania
source: Hawkes, K., O'Connell, J. F., Blurton Jones, N. G., Alvarez, H., and Charnov, E. L. (1998). Grandmothering, menopause, and the evolution of human life histories. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 95(3), 1336-1339.
caveat: The grandmother hypothesis remains debated among anthropologists, and other explanations for long human lifespans have been proposed.
